doc.title: Chuck Lamb interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, February 7, 2023

title: Wrong notes and playing with Diego Figueiredo
summary: Lamb says there are no wrong notes in improvisation, and discusses his rapport with guitarist Diego Figueiredo.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Are there wrong notes in improvising?

No. Because you — I mean so if I’m improvising on something and there’s not a lot of thought going on you’re just really following the flow of what’s happening and then if I’ll go up to what would be a wrong note I would just change what I’m doing for it to match. Like if it’s a half step above — not to get, you know — but you just navigate what that note is, you navigate if another player does something funky like that, go ahead and grab it and make it a like oh my God that was brilliant you know. You could reharmonize it to — and you know you’re working like that and if you’re working with players on that level it’s like that’s the coolest stuff on a gig when that happens.
I heard you do that last night, believe it or not. I was watching the video from Small’s where you were playing with Diego. How do you pronounce his last name?
And that was happening I think, and he would do something and almost instantaneously you played in a fashion that enhanced or went with it. And vice versa when you started playing.

Yeah he’s a cat that — that connection is very deep like that. It was from the first time we played, we both recognized that, I mean culturally very different upbringings but the improv thing, the freedom improv thing just jelled with us.

There was a part in the middle of it where I suggest people get on the Internet and try to find it, where it was like you turned into J.S. Bach for a little while. It was sort of a contrapuntal two thing. But going back to the wrong note business, and I wish I could think of a better term than wrong — unintended perhaps. If you’re playing with other people, bass and guitar especially, and they’re playing the changes, do you play differently than if you were playing the same song but by yourself?

Yeah. I do. But, because we’re following a script. But you know that’s interesting I’m just thinking are there any wrong notes, yes there are. The bass player could play — there’s mistakes but in looking at your question, depending on these musicians, so you’re following the script but if you still start — you start pushing it around all the musicians will follow the improv you know. So it does have — it still has that same freedom, you’re taking a little bit more of a risk by pushing outside the boundaries of what you have on the script and hopefully guys will come with you or at least give you the room to do that. Does that make sense?
Yeah. When you turn to the piano to play something unknown, do your hands just — I’m trying to rephrase here — does your mind direct your hands or is it the other way around?
